However, since then, my head has felt very cloudy and I keep losing track of what I'm doing in the middle of everyday things, like following a recipe or reading scripture at Bible study.\n\nDoctor: Can you describe more about what you mean by feeling 'detached from your family' and 'moving through a foggy dream', is it like you're observing yourself and your life from outside your body or more like you're just feeling disconnected from your emotions and surroundings?\n\nPatient: It is actually both. On one hand, I feel like I'm moving through a foggy dream where my own house and hands don't feel real, as if I'm watching my life from a distance. At the same time, I feel emotionally flat and disconnected, unable to feel the joy I know I should feel when my grandchildren come to visit.\n\nDoctor: Have you experienced any flashbacks, nightmares, or intense reactions to reminders of the car accident, or is your distress more focused on the memory gap and feeling disconnected from your life?\n\nPatient: No, I don’t have nightmares or vivid flashbacks of the crash itself. My distress is really focused on that frustrating blank space in my memory where the accident should be, and feeling so deeply disconnected from my life, like I'm moving through a foggy dream and can't feel my emotions normally.\n\nDoctor: Can you tell me if you've had any experiences where you've done something or gone somewhere and then later couldn't recall how you got there or what you did, since the accident?\n\nPatient: No, I haven't had any experiences where I went somewhere or did something and completely forgot how I got there. While I do lose my train of thought easily and still have that blank spot from the accident itself, I don't lose track of my physical location or my actions in that way.\n\nDoctor: Can you tell me if your inability to recall the accident is the only specific event you're unable to remember, or are there other specific events or periods of time since the accident that you also can't recall?\n\nPatient: Yes, that chunk of time during the accident itself is the only specific event I cannot recall. While my head gets very cloudy and I lose track of what I'm doing during daily tasks, I haven't forgotten any other events or periods of time since the crash.\n\nDoctor: Have you experienced any episodes where you felt like you were a different person or had a different identity, or where things around you seemed unreal, since the accident?\n\nPatient: I haven't felt like a different person, but things around me definitely seem unreal. Quite often, it feels like I'm moving through a foggy dream, and even my own house and hands don't feel like they belong to me. It is as if I am just watching my life happen from a distance.\n\nDoctor: Can you clarify if the feeling of being in a 'foggy dream' and being detached from your life and emotions is constant since the accident, or does it come and go?\n\nPatient: These feelings have been very persistent and haven't really let up since the accident a little over two weeks ago. While it is especially noticeable when I am trying to interact with my family or do my daily activities, it feels like a constant heavy fog in the background rather than something that easily comes and goes.\n\nDoctor: Can you estimate how much of your daily life, since the accident, has been spent feeling like you're in this 'foggy dream' state or detached from your emotions and surroundings?\n\nPatient: I would say I feel this way quite often, almost constantly since the accident a little over two weeks ago. It truly feels like I am just watching my life from a distance rather than actually experiencing it.\n\nDoctor: Can you describe if the feeling of being detached from yourself and your surroundings, like you're watching your life from a distance, is more distressing to you than the memory gap of the accident itself?\n\nPatient: They are both very distressing, but in different ways. However, since then, my head has felt very cloudy and I keep losing track of what I'm doing in the middle of everyday things, like following a recipe or reading scripture at Bible study.\n\nDoctor: Can you describe more about what you mean by feeling 'detached from your family' and 'moving through a foggy dream', is it like you're observing yourself and your life from outside your body or more like you're just feeling disconnected from your emotions and surroundings?\n\nPatient: It is actually both. On one hand, I feel like I'm moving through a foggy dream where my own house and hands don't feel real, as if I'm watching my life from a distance. At the same time, I feel emotionally flat and disconnected, unable to feel the joy I know I should feel when my grandchildren come to visit.\n\nDoctor: Have you experienced any flashbacks, nightmares, or intense reactions to reminders of the car accident, or is your distress more focused on the memory gap and feeling disconnected from your life?\n\nPatient: No, I don’t have nightmares or vivid flashbacks of the crash itself. My distress is really focused on that frustrating blank space in my memory where the accident should be, and feeling so deeply disconnected from my life, like I'm moving through a foggy dream and can't feel my emotions normally.\n\nDoctor: Can you tell me if you've had any experiences where you've done something or gone somewhere and then later couldn't recall how you got there or what you did, since the accident?\n\nPatient: No, I haven't had any experiences where I went somewhere or did something and completely forgot how I got there. While I do lose my train of thought easily and still have that blank spot from the accident itself, I don't lose track of my physical location or my actions in that way.\n\nDoctor: Can you tell me if your inability to recall the accident is the only specific event you're unable to remember, or are there other specific events or periods of time since the accident that you also can't recall?\n\nPatient: Yes, that chunk of time during the accident itself is the only specific event I cannot recall. While my head gets very cloudy and I lose track of what I'm doing during daily tasks, I haven't forgotten any other events or periods of time since the crash.\n\nDoctor: Have you experienced any episodes where you felt like you were a different person or had a different identity, or where things around you seemed unreal, since the accident?\n\nPatient: I haven't felt like a different person, but things around me definitely seem unreal. Quite often, it feels like I'm moving through a foggy dream, and even my own house and hands don't feel like they belong to me. It is as if I am just watching my life happen from a distance.\n\nDoctor: Can you clarify if the feeling of being in a 'foggy dream' and being detached from your life and emotions is constant since the accident, or does it come and go?\n\nPatient: These feelings have been very persistent and haven't really let up since the accident a little over two weeks ago. While it is especially noticeable when I am trying to interact with my family or do my daily activities, it feels like a constant heavy fog in the background rather than something that easily comes and goes.\n\nDoctor: Can you estimate how much of your daily life, since the accident, has been spent feeling like you're in this 'foggy dream' state or detached from your emotions and surroundings?\n\nPatient: I would say I feel this way quite often, almost constantly since the accident a little over two weeks ago. The memory gap is deeply frustrating because it constantly bothers me that there is just this empty hole where that night should be, while the foggy dream is highly unsettling because it makes me feel so disconnected from my own home and family.\n\nDoctor: Can you tell me if you've experienced any significant avoidance of people, places, or activities that remind you of the car accident, or is your main distress focused on the memory gap and feeling disconnected?\n\nPatient: I definitely avoid a lot of things now, like refusing to take the route where the crash happened, only riding in the car if my daughter takes side streets, and stopping my senior classes and walking club. At the same time, I feel emotionally flat and disconnected, unable to feel the joy I know I should feel when my grandchildren come to visit.\n\nDoctor: Have you experienced any flashbacks, nightmares, or intense reactions to reminders of the car accident, or is your distress more focused on the memory gap and feeling disconnected from your life?\n\nPatient: No, I don’t have nightmares or vivid flashbacks of the crash itself. My distress is really focused on that frustrating blank space in my memory where the accident should be, and feeling so deeply disconnected from my life, like I'm moving through a foggy dream and can't feel my emotions normally.\n\nDoctor: Can you tell me if you've had any experiences where you've done something or gone somewhere and then later couldn't recall how you got there or what you did, since the accident?\n\nPatient: No, I haven't had any experiences where I went somewhere or did something and completely forgot how I got there. While I do lose my train of thought easily and still have that blank spot from the accident itself, I don't lose track of my physical location or my actions in that way.\n\nDoctor: Can you tell me if your inability to recall the accident is the only specific event you're unable to remember, or are there other specific events or periods of time since the accident that you also can't recall?\n\nPatient: Yes, that chunk of time during the accident itself is the only specific event I cannot recall. While my head gets very cloudy and I lose track of what I'm doing during daily tasks, I haven't forgotten any other events or periods of time since the crash.\n\nDoctor: Have you experienced any episodes where you felt like you were a different person or had a different identity, or where things around you seemed unreal, since the accident?\n\nPatient: I haven't felt like a different person, but things around me definitely seem unreal. Quite often, it feels like I'm moving through a foggy dream, and even my own house and hands don't feel like they belong to me. It is as if I am just watching my life happen from a distance.\n\nDoctor: Can you clarify if the feeling of being in a 'foggy dream' and being detached from your life and emotions is constant since the accident, or does it come and go?\n\nPatient: These feelings have been very persistent and haven't really let up since the accident a little over two weeks ago. While it is especially noticeable when I am trying to interact with my family or do my daily activities, it feels like a constant heavy fog in the background rather than something that easily comes and goes.\n\nDoctor: Can you estimate how much of your daily life, since the accident, has been spent feeling like you're in this 'foggy dream' state or detached from your emotions and surroundings?\n\nPatient: I would say I feel this way quite often, almost constantly since the accident a little over two weeks ago. I feel like I am moving through this foggy dream quite often, and these feelings haven't really let up at all over the past few weeks.\n\nDoctor: Can you describe how your emotional flatness and detachment from your life affect your ability to experience positive emotions, such as happiness or love, towards your family and loved ones?\n\nPatient: When my children and grandchildren come over to try and cheer me up, I just feel completely flat and far away, as if I am watching someone else's family. While my head gets very cloudy and I lose track of what I'm doing during daily tasks, I haven't forgotten any other events or periods of time since the crash.\n\nDoctor: Have you experienced any episodes where you felt like you were a different person or had a different identity, or where things around you seemed unreal, since the accident?\n\nPatient: I haven't felt like a different person, but things around me definitely seem unreal. It just feels like I am constantly watching my life from a distance during my daily routine.\n\nDoctor: Do you feel like the foggy dream state and detachment from your life are directly triggered by reminders of the accident, or are they more of a constant, background feeling that you've had since the accident?\n\nPatient: It is definitely more of a constant, background feeling that has been there almost all the time, rather than just being triggered by reminders of the crash. I feel like I am moving through this foggy dream quite often, and these feelings haven't really let up at all over the past few weeks.\n\nDoctor: Can you describe how your emotional flatness and detachment from your life affect your ability to experience positive emotions, such as happiness or love, towards your family and loved ones?\n\nPatient: When my children and grandchildren come over to try and cheer me up, I just feel completely flat and far away, as if I am watching someone else's family. Because of that, it has been very difficult to feel fully connected to my surroundings lately.\n\nDoctor: Can you tell me if the feeling of being detached from yourself and your life is more related to the memory gap of the accident, or if it's a separate experience that you're having?\n\nPatient: They feel like two separate, troubling experiences that both started after the accident. I can’t remember important parts of the crash, and it really bothers me that there’s just this blank where that night should be.\n\nDoctor: Can you tell me more about what you mean by 'important parts of the crash' that you can't remember, and have you experienced any other unusual symptoms or feelings since the accident?\n\nPatient: There is a big empty space between seeing that car slide toward us on the ice and suddenly being outside on the road with people talking to me. Since then, I feel like I'm moving through a foggy dream, completely detached from my family, and I've become so jumpy and anxious that I've stopped going to my senior classes and walkers club.\n\nDoctor: Can you tell me if your inability to recall parts of the accident is the only memory problem you're experiencing, or have you noticed any difficulty remembering things that happened before or after the accident?\n\nPatient: My memory of everything before the accident is perfectly fine, and the blank is strictly that gap during the crash itself. However, since then, my head has felt very cloudy and I keep losing track of what I'm doing in the middle of everyday things, like following a recipe or reading scripture at Bible study.\n\nDoctor: Can you describe more about what you mean by feeling 'detached from your family' and 'moving through a foggy dream', is it like you're observing yourself and your life from outside your body or more like you're just feeling disconnected from your emotions and surroundings?\n\nPatient: It is actually both. On one hand, I feel like I'm moving through a foggy dream where my own house and hands don't feel real, as if I'm watching my life from a distance. At the same time, I feel emotionally flat and disconnected, unable to feel the joy I know I should feel when my grandchildren come to visit.\n\nDoctor: Have you experienced any flashbacks, nightmares, or intense reactions to reminders of the car accident, or is your distress more focused on the memory gap and feeling disconnected from your life?\n\nPatient: No, I don’t have nightmares or vivid flashbacks of the crash itself. My distress is really focused on that frustrating blank space in my memory where the accident should be, and feeling so deeply disconnected from my life, like I'm moving through a foggy dream and can't feel my emotions normally.\n\nDoctor: Can you tell me if you've had any experiences where you've done something or gone somewhere and then later couldn't recall how you got there or what you did, since the accident?\n\nPatient: No, I haven't had any experiences where I went somewhere or did something and completely forgot how I got there. While I do lose my train of thought easily and still have that blank spot from the accident itself, I don't lose track of my physical location or my actions in that way.\n\nDoctor: Can you tell me if your inability to recall the accident is the only specific event you're unable to remember, or are there other specific events or periods of time since the accident that you also can't recall?\n\nPatient: Yes, that chunk of time during the accident itself is the only specific event I cannot recall. While my head gets very cloudy and I lose track of what I'm doing during daily tasks, I haven't forgotten any other events or periods of time since the crash.\n\nDoctor: Have you experienced any episodes where you felt like you were a different person or had a different identity, or where things around you seemed unreal, since the accident?\n\nPatient: I haven't felt like a different person, but things around me definitely seem unreal. Quite often, it feels like I'm moving through a foggy dream, and even my own house and hands don't feel like they belong to me. It is as if I am just watching my life happen from a distance.\n\nDoctor: Can you clarify if the feeling of being in a 'foggy dream' and being detached from your life and emotions is constant since the accident, or does it come and go?\n\nPatient: These feelings have been very persistent and haven't really let up since the accident a little over two weeks ago. While it is especially noticeable when I am trying to interact with my family or do my daily activities, it feels like a constant heavy fog in the background rather than something that easily comes and goes.\n\nDoctor: Can you estimate how much of your daily life, since the accident, has been spent feeling like you're in this 'foggy dream' state or detached from your emotions and surroundings?\n\nPatient: I would say I feel this way quite often, almost constantly since the accident a little over two weeks ago. For most of the day, I am moving through that foggy dream, feeling completely flat and detached from my family. It truly feels like I am just watching my life from a distance rather than actually experiencing it.\n\nDoctor: Can you describe if the feeling of being detached from yourself and your surroundings, like you're watching your life from a distance, is more distressing to you than the memory gap of the accident itself?\n\nPatient: They are both very distressing, but in different ways. The memory gap is deeply frustrating because it constantly bothers me that there is just this empty hole where that night should be, while the foggy dream is highly unsettling because it makes me feel so disconnected from my own home and family.\n\nDoctor: Can you tell me if you've experienced any significant avoidance of people, places, or activities that remind you of the car accident, or is your main distress focused on the memory gap and feeling disconnected?\n\nPatient: I definitely avoid a lot of things now, like refusing to take the route where the crash happened, only riding in the car if my daughter takes side streets, and stopping my senior classes and walking club. At the same time, that empty memory blank and feeling constantly disconnected and foggy in a dream are also deeply distressing to me.\n\nDoctor: Can you clarify if the feeling of being in a 'foggy dream' and detached from your life is primarily related to the memory gap of the accident, or if it's a more general feeling that persists even when you're not thinking about the accident?\n\nPatient: It is definitely a more general, persistent feeling that stays with me throughout the day, even when I am not thinking about the accident. I can be doing normal things like looking at my own hands in my house, or trying to follow a recipe or a passage at Bible study, and everything still feels completely unreal. It just feels like I am constantly watching my life from a distance during my daily routine.\n\nDoctor: Do you feel like the foggy dream state and detachment from your life are directly triggered by reminders of the accident, or are they more of a constant, background feeling that you've had since the accident?\n\nPatient: It is definitely more of a constant, background feeling that has been there almost all the time, rather than just being triggered by reminders of the crash. I feel like I am moving through this foggy dream quite often, and these feelings haven't really let up at all over the past few weeks.\n\nDoctor: Can you describe how your emotional flatness and detachment from your life affect your ability to experience positive emotions, such as happiness or love, towards your family and loved ones?\n\nPatient: When my children and grandchildren come over to try and cheer me up, I just feel completely flat and far away, as if I am watching someone else's family. I know I should feel happy and loving toward them, but I simply cannot feel the joy I am supposed to feel.\n\nDoctor: Can you describe if there are any moments or activities where you feel fully connected to yourself and your surroundings, or if the feeling of detachment and being in a 'foggy dream' is always present?\n\nPatient: While it might not be literally every second, this foggy dream feeling happens quite often during the day. It feels like I'm watching my life from a distance, and even my own hands and house don't feel like they truly belong to me. Because of that, it has been very difficult to feel fully connected to my surroundings lately.\n\nDoctor: Can you tell me if the feeling of being detached from yourself and your life is more related to the memory gap of the accident, or if it's a separate experience that you're having?\n\nPatient: They feel like two separate, troubling experiences that both started after the accident. The memory gap is a specific blank space concerning the night of the crash itself, whereas the detached, dream-like feeling is an ongoing daily experience where I feel disconnected from my own body and surroundings, as if watching my life from a distance.\n\nDoctor: Can you clarify if the feeling of being detached from yourself and your life, like you're watching it from a distance, is the same as the feeling you have when you try to remember the accident, or are these two distinct feelings for you?\n\nPatient: Yes, they are two very distinct feelings for me. Trying to remember the accident feels like hitting a big empty space where the memories should be, which is deeply frustrating. In contrast, the detachment is like moving through a foggy dream where my own hands and house don't feel real, as if I am watching my life from a distance.\n\nDoctor: Can you confirm whether the detached, dream-like feeling you experience is related to a specific aspect of your identity or sense of self, or if it's more of a general disconnection from your daily life and surroundings?\n\nPatient: I believe it is a mix of both, dear. On one hand, my surroundings like my house feel like a foggy dream that isn't quite real. But on the other hand, my own hands don't feel like they belong to me, and I feel like I'm just watching my life from a distance.\n\nDoctor: Can you describe if there are any specific aspects of your identity or sense of self that feel altered or unreal to you, beyond just the general feeling of detachment and being in a 'foggy dream'?\n\nPatient: Yes, it is my own body that feels so disconnected. I will look down at my own hands and feel like they aren't mine, and I often catch myself thinking, \"Is this really happening to me?\" as I watch my life from a distance.\n\nDoctor: Have you ever felt like you're going to snap out of this foggy dream state, or does it feel like it's going to be a permanent part of your life now?"

At the same time, that empty memory blank and feeling constantly disconnected and foggy in a dream are also deeply distressing to me.\n\nDoctor: Can you clarify if the feeling of being in a 'foggy dream' and detached from your life is primarily related to the memory gap of the accident, or if it's a more general feeling that persists even when you're not thinking about the accident?\n\nPatient: It is definitely a more general, persistent feeling that stays with me throughout the day, even when I am not thinking about the accident. I can be doing normal things like looking at my own hands in my house, or trying to follow a recipe or a passage at Bible study, and everything still feels completely unreal. It just feels like I am constantly watching my life from a distance during my daily routine.\n\nDoctor: Do you feel like the foggy dream state and detachment from your life are directly triggered by reminders of the accident, or are they more of a constant, background feeling that you've had since the accident?\n\nPatient: It is definitely more of a constant, background feeling that has been there almost all the time, rather than just being triggered by reminders of the crash. I feel like I am moving through this foggy dream quite often, and these feelings haven't really let up at all over the past few weeks.\n\nDoctor: Can you describe how your emotional flatness and detachment from your life affect your ability to experience positive emotions, such as happiness or love, towards your family and loved ones?\n\nPatient: When my children and grandchildren come over to try and cheer me up, I just feel completely flat and far away, as if I am watching someone else's family. I know I should feel happy and loving toward them, but I simply cannot feel the joy I am supposed to feel.\n\nDoctor: Can you describe if there are any moments or activities where you feel fully connected to yourself and your surroundings, or if the feeling of detachment and being in a 'foggy dream' is always present?\n\nPatient: While it might not be literally every second, this foggy dream feeling happens quite often during the day. The memory gap is a specific blank space concerning the night of the crash itself, whereas the detached, dream-like feeling is an ongoing daily experience where I feel disconnected from my own body and surroundings, as if watching my life from a distance.\n\nDoctor: Can you clarify if the feeling of being detached from yourself and your life, like you're watching it from a distance, is the same as the feeling you have when you try to remember the accident, or are these two distinct feelings for you?\n\nPatient: Yes, they are two very distinct feelings for me. On one hand, my surroundings like my house feel like a foggy dream that isn't quite real. But on the other hand, my own hands don't feel like they belong to me, and I feel like I'm just watching my life from a distance.\n\nDoctor: Can you describe if there are any specific aspects of your identity or sense of self that feel altered or unreal to you, beyond just the general feeling of detachment and being in a 'foggy dream'?\n\nPatient: Yes, it is my own body that feels so disconnected. I will look down at my own hands and feel like they aren't mine, and I often catch myself thinking, \"Is this really happening to me?\" as I watch my life from a distance.\n\nDoctor: Have you ever felt like you're going to snap out of this foggy dream state, or does it feel like it's going to be a permanent part of your life now?\n\nPatient: No, it doesn't feel like I am going to snap out of it, because this foggy dream has been happening constantly ever since the accident a little over two weeks ago without letting up. Since it hasn't improved at all, I am starting to worry that it might never go away. It is very worrying to think this might be how things are from now on."

I can be doing normal things like looking at my own hands in my house, or trying to follow a recipe or a passage at Bible study, and everything still feels completely unreal. It just feels like I am constantly watching my life from a distance during my daily routine.\n\nDoctor: Do you feel like the foggy dream state and detachment from your life are directly triggered by reminders of the accident, or are they more of a constant, background feeling that you've had since the accident?\n\nPatient: It is definitely more of a constant, background feeling that has been there almost all the time, rather than just being triggered by reminders of the crash. I feel like I am moving through this foggy dream quite often, and these feelings haven't really let up at all over the past few weeks.\n\nDoctor: Can you describe how your emotional flatness and detachment from your life affect your ability to experience positive emotions, such as happiness or love, towards your family and loved ones?\n\nPatient: When my children and grandchildren come over to try and cheer me up, I just feel completely flat and far away, as if I am watching someone else's family. I know I should feel happy and loving toward them, but I simply cannot feel the joy I am supposed to feel.\n\nDoctor: Can you describe if there are any moments or activities where you feel fully connected to yourself and your surroundings, or if the feeling of detachment and being in a 'foggy dream' is always present?\n\nPatient: While it might not be literally every second, this foggy dream feeling happens quite often during the day. It feels like I'm watching my life from a distance, and even my own hands and house don't feel like they truly belong to me. The memory gap is a specific blank space concerning the night of the crash itself, whereas the detached, dream-like feeling is an ongoing daily experience where I feel disconnected from my own body and surroundings, as if watching my life from a distance.\n\nDoctor: Can you clarify if the feeling of being detached from yourself and your life, like you're watching it from a distance, is the same as the feeling you have when you try to remember the accident, or are these two distinct feelings for you?\n\nPatient: Yes, they are two very distinct feelings for me. Trying to remember the accident feels like hitting a big empty space where the memories should be, which is deeply frustrating. In contrast, the detachment is like moving through a foggy dream where my own hands and house don't feel real, as if I am watching my life from a distance.\n\nDoctor: Can you confirm whether the detached, dream-like feeling you experience is related to a specific aspect of your identity or sense of self, or if it's more of a general disconnection from your daily life and surroundings?\n\nPatient: I believe it is a mix of both, dear. I will look down at my own hands and feel like they aren't mine, and I often catch myself thinking, \"Is this really happening to me?\" as I watch my life from a distance.\n\nDoctor: Have you ever felt like you're going to snap out of this foggy dream state, or does it feel like it's going to be a permanent part of your life now?\n\nPatient: No, it doesn't feel like I am going to snap out of it, because this foggy dream has been happening constantly ever since the accident a little over two weeks ago without letting up. Since it hasn't improved at all, I am starting to worry that it might never go away. It is very worrying to think this might be how things are from now on.\n\nDoctor: Can you tell me if the feeling of detachment from your body and surroundings is more bothersome to you than the memory gap of the accident, or are they equally distressing in different ways?\n\nPatient: They are both deeply distressing to me, just in very different ways, dear. The memory gap is so frustrating because I keep trying to replay the accident in my mind, but there's just this blank space where it should be. The detachment is so unsettling and surreal, like I'm moving through a foggy dream and watching my life from a distance.\n\nDoctor: Can you tell me if your feeling of being detached from your life and body is something that you feel is happening to you, or if it's something that you're observing from outside, and is this feeling related to the memory gap of the accident or a separate experience?"

I know I should feel happy and loving toward them, but I simply cannot feel the joy I am supposed to feel.\n\nDoctor: Can you describe if there are any moments or activities where you feel fully connected to yourself and your surroundings, or if the feeling of detachment and being in a 'foggy dream' is always present?\n\nPatient: While it might not be literally every second, this foggy dream feeling happens quite often during the day. In contrast, the detachment is like moving through a foggy dream where my own hands and house don't feel real, as if I am watching my life from a distance.\n\nDoctor: Can you confirm whether the detached, dream-like feeling you experience is related to a specific aspect of your identity or sense of self, or if it's more of a general disconnection from your daily life and surroundings?\n\nPatient: I believe it is a mix of both, dear. On one hand, my surroundings like my house feel like a foggy dream that isn't quite real. But on the other hand, my own hands don't feel like they belong to me, and I feel like I'm just watching my life from a distance.\n\nDoctor: Can you describe if there are any specific aspects of your identity or sense of self that feel altered or unreal to you, beyond just the general feeling of detachment and being in a 'foggy dream'?\n\nPatient: Yes, it is my own body that feels so disconnected. I will look down at my own hands and feel like they aren't mine, and I often catch myself thinking, \"Is this really happening to me?\" as I watch my life from a distance.\n\nDoctor: Have you ever felt like you're going to snap out of this foggy dream state, or does it feel like it's going to be a permanent part of your life now?\n\nPatient: No, it doesn't feel like I am going to snap out of it, because this foggy dream has been happening constantly ever since the accident a little over two weeks ago without letting up. Since it hasn't improved at all, I am starting to worry that it might never go away. It is very worrying to think this might be how things are from now on.\n\nDoctor: Can you tell me if the feeling of detachment from your body and surroundings is more bothersome to you than the memory gap of the accident, or are they equally distressing in different ways?\n\nPatient: They are both deeply distressing to me, just in very different ways, dear. While my head gets very cloudy and I lose track of what I'm doing during daily tasks, I haven't forgotten any other events or periods of time since the crash.\n\nDoctor: Have you experienced any episodes where you felt like you were a different person or had a different identity, or where things around you seemed unreal, since the accident?\n\nPatient: I haven't felt like a different person, but things around me definitely seem unreal. Quite often, it feels like I'm moving through a foggy dream, and even my own house and hands don't feel like they belong to me. It is as if I am just watching my life happen from a distance.\n\nDoctor: Can you clarify if the feeling of being in a 'foggy dream' and being detached from your life and emotions is constant since the accident, or does it come and go?\n\nPatient: These feelings have been very persistent and haven't really let up since the accident a little over two weeks ago. While it is especially noticeable when I am trying to interact with my family or do my daily activities, it feels like a constant heavy fog in the background rather than something that easily comes and goes.\n\nDoctor: Can you estimate how much of your daily life, since the accident, has been spent feeling like you're in this 'foggy dream' state or detached from your emotions and surroundings?\n\nPatient: I would say I feel this way quite often, almost constantly since the accident a little over two weeks ago. For most of the day, I am moving through that foggy dream, feeling completely flat and detached from my family. It truly feels like I am just watching my life from a distance rather than actually experiencing it.\n\nDoctor: Can you describe if the feeling of being detached from yourself and your surroundings, like you're watching your life from a distance, is more distressing to you than the memory gap of the accident itself?\n\nPatient: They are both very distressing, but in different ways. The memory gap is deeply frustrating because it constantly bothers me that there is just this empty hole where that night should be, while the foggy dream is highly unsettling because it makes me feel so disconnected from my own home and family.\n\nDoctor: Can you tell me if you've experienced any significant avoidance of people, places, or activities that remind you of the car accident, or is your main distress focused on the memory gap and feeling disconnected?\n\nPatient: I definitely avoid a lot of things now, like refusing to take the route where the crash happened, only riding in the car if my daughter takes side streets, and stopping my senior classes and walking club. At the same time, that empty memory blank and feeling constantly disconnected and foggy in a dream are also deeply distressing to me.\n\nDoctor: Can you clarify if the feeling of being in a 'foggy dream' and detached from your life is primarily related to the memory gap of the accident, or if it's a more general feeling that persists even when you're not thinking about the accident?\n\nPatient: It is definitely a more general, persistent feeling that stays with me throughout the day, even when I am not thinking about the accident. I can be doing normal things like looking at my own hands in my house, or trying to follow a recipe or a passage at Bible study, and everything still feels completely unreal. It just feels like I am constantly watching my life from a distance during my daily routine.\n\nDoctor: Do you feel like the foggy dream state and detachment from your life are directly triggered by reminders of the accident, or are they more of a constant, background feeling that you've had since the accident?\n\nPatient: It is definitely more of a constant, background feeling that has been there almost all the time, rather than just being triggered by reminders of the crash. I feel like I am moving through this foggy dream quite often, and these feelings haven't really let up at all over the past few weeks.\n\nDoctor: Can you describe how your emotional flatness and detachment from your life affect your ability to experience positive emotions, such as happiness or love, towards your family and loved ones?\n\nPatient: When my children and grandchildren come over to try and cheer me up, I just feel completely flat and far away, as if I am watching someone else's family. I know I should feel happy and loving toward them, but I simply cannot feel the joy I am supposed to feel.\n\nDoctor: Can you describe if there are any moments or activities where you feel fully connected to yourself and your surroundings, or if the feeling of detachment and being in a 'foggy dream' is always present?\n\nPatient: While it might not be literally every second, this foggy dream feeling happens quite often during the day. It feels like I'm watching my life from a distance, and even my own hands and house don't feel like they truly belong to me. Because of that, it has been very difficult to feel fully connected to my surroundings lately.\n\nDoctor: Can you tell me if the feeling of being detached from yourself and your life is more related to the memory gap of the accident, or if it's a separate experience that you're having?\n\nPatient: They feel like two separate, troubling experiences that both started after the accident. The memory gap is a specific blank space concerning the night of the crash itself, whereas the detached, dream-like feeling is an ongoing daily experience where I feel disconnected from my own body and surroundings, as if watching my life from a distance.\n\nDoctor: Can you clarify if the feeling of being detached from yourself and your life, like you're watching it from a distance, is the same as the feeling you have when you try to remember the accident, or are these two distinct feelings for you?\n\nPatient: Yes, they are two very distinct feelings for me. Trying to remember the accident feels like hitting a big empty space where the memories should be, which is deeply frustrating. In contrast, the detachment is like moving through a foggy dream where my own hands and house don't feel real, as if I am watching my life from a distance.\n\nDoctor: Can you confirm whether the detached, dream-like feeling you experience is related to a specific aspect of your identity or sense of self, or if it's more of a general disconnection from your daily life and surroundings?\n\nPatient: I believe it is a mix of both, dear. On one hand, my surroundings like my house feel like a foggy dream that isn't quite real. But on the other hand, my own hands don't feel like they belong to me, and I feel like I'm just watching my life from a distance.\n\nDoctor: Can you describe if there are any specific aspects of your identity or sense of self that feel altered or unreal to you, beyond just the general feeling of detachment and being in a 'foggy dream'?\n\nPatient: Yes, it is my own body that feels so disconnected. I will look down at my own hands and feel like they aren't mine, and I often catch myself thinking, \"Is this really happening to me?\" as I watch my life from a distance.\n\nDoctor: Have you ever felt like you're going to snap out of this foggy dream state, or does it feel like it's going to be a permanent part of your life now?\n\nPatient: No, it doesn't feel like I am going to snap out of it, because this foggy dream has been happening constantly ever since the accident a little over two weeks ago without letting up. Since it hasn't improved at all, I am starting to worry that it might never go away. It is very worrying to think this might be how things are from now on.\n\nDoctor: Can you tell me if the feeling of detachment from your body and surroundings is more bothersome to you than the memory gap of the accident, or are they equally distressing in different ways?\n\nPatient: They are both deeply distressing to me, just in very different ways, dear. The memory gap is so frustrating because I keep trying to replay the accident in my mind, but there's just this blank space where it should be. The detachment is so unsettling and surreal, like I'm moving through a foggy dream and watching my life from a distance.\n\nDoctor: Can you tell me if your feeling of being detached from your life and body is something that you feel is happening to you, or if it's something that you're observing from outside, and is this feeling related to the memory gap of the accident or a separate experience?\n\nPatient: It feels like I am observing my life from the outside, moving through a foggy dream where even my own hands don't feel like they belong to me. While both started after the crash, they feel like separate experiences to me. The memory gap is just a specific blank space about the accident itself, whereas this detachment is an ongoing, daily feeling of unreality.\n\nDoctor: Have you experienced any moments where you felt like you were going to return to normal, or does the feeling of detachment and being in a 'foggy dream' feel like it's become your new normal?\n\nPatient: Unfortunately, yes, this foggy and detached feeling has become my new normal, and it hasn't let up at all since the accident over two weeks ago. I constantly feel like I am moving through a dream, watching my life from a distance. I don't have any moments where I feel back to my old self anymore.\n\nDoctor: Can you tell me if there are any specific times or situations when your feeling of detachment and being in a 'foggy dream' is more or less pronounced, and does this feeling ever intersect with your attempts to recall the memory gap of the accident?\n\nPatient: Yes, that foggy, dream-like feeling actually becomes much more intense whenever I try to think about the accident or when people ask me about it. Whenever I try to force my mind to replay the crash to fill in that blank space, I find myself slipping deeper into that detached state, as if my mind is drifting away to protect itself. It just leaves me completely unable to grasp the memory.\n\nDoctor: Can you describe if there are any times when you feel like you're reliving the accident or any part of it, even if it's not a clear memory, or if your experiences since the accident have been more about feeling disconnected and unable to recall the event?\n\nPatient: My experience is definitely much more about feeling disconnected and being unable to recall the event rather than actively reliving it. I don't have vivid flashbacks of the crash, but instead face a frustrating blank space whenever I try to remember what happened. Mostly, I just feel detached, like I am moving through a foggy dream and watching my life from a distance.\n\nDoctor: Can you tell me if you have ever experienced a period where you felt like you were someone else or had a different identity, or if the feeling of detachment is primarily related to your surroundings and daily life rather than your sense of self?\n\nPatient: No, I have never felt like a different person or had a different identity. Instead, the detachment makes me feel like I am moving through a foggy dream where my surroundings, like my house, and even my own hands don't feel like they belong to me, as if I am watching my life from a distance.\n\nDoctor: Can you tell me if the feeling of detachment and being in a 'foggy dream' is more closely related to your inability to recall the accident, or if it's a distinct experience that affects your daily life and sense of identity?\n\nPatient: While they are both deeply unsettling, they feel like two distinct experiences to me. The foggy dream is an ongoing, daily feeling where I feel completely disconnected from my own body, hands, and home, as if watching my life from a distance. On the other hand, the memory loss is a specific, frustrating blank spot that is strictly limited to the moments of the crash itself.\n\nDoctor: Can you tell me if the feeling of being in a 'foggy dream' and detached from your life is something that you feel is a result of trying to cope with the memory gap of the accident, or if it's a separate experience that you're having, unrelated to your attempts to recall the accident?"

While I do lose my train of thought easily and still have that blank spot from the accident itself, I don't lose track of my physical location or my actions in that way.\n\nDoctor: Can you tell me if your inability to recall the accident is the only specific event you're unable to remember, or are there other specific events or periods of time since the accident that you also can't recall?\n\nPatient: Yes, that chunk of time during the accident itself is the only specific event I cannot recall. While my head gets very cloudy and I lose track of what I'm doing during daily tasks, I haven't forgotten any other events or periods of time since the crash.\n\nDoctor: Have you experienced any episodes where you felt like you were a different person or had a different identity, or where things around you seemed unreal, since the accident?\n\nPatient: I haven't felt like a different person, but things around me definitely seem unreal. Quite often, it feels like I'm moving through a foggy dream, and even my own house and hands don't feel like they belong to me. It is as if I am just watching my life happen from a distance.\n\nDoctor: Can you clarify if the feeling of being in a 'foggy dream' and being detached from your life and emotions is constant since the accident, or does it come and go?\n\nPatient: These feelings have been very persistent and haven't really let up since the accident a little over two weeks ago. While it is especially noticeable when I am trying to interact with my family or do my daily activities, it feels like a constant heavy fog in the background rather than something that easily comes and goes.\n\nDoctor: Can you estimate how much of your daily life, since the accident, has been spent feeling like you're in this 'foggy dream' state or detached from your emotions and surroundings?\n\nPatient: I would say I feel this way quite often, almost constantly since the accident a little over two weeks ago. For most of the day, I am moving through that foggy dream, feeling completely flat and detached from my family. It truly feels like I am just watching my life from a distance rather than actually experiencing it.\n\nDoctor: Can you describe if the feeling of being detached from yourself and your surroundings, like you're watching your life from a distance, is more distressing to you than the memory gap of the accident itself?\n\nPatient: They are both very distressing, but in different ways. The memory gap is deeply frustrating because it constantly bothers me that there is just this empty hole where that night should be, while the foggy dream is highly unsettling because it makes me feel so disconnected from my own home and family.\n\nDoctor: Can you tell me if you've experienced any significant avoidance of people, places, or activities that remind you of the car accident, or is your main distress focused on the memory gap and feeling disconnected?\n\nPatient: I definitely avoid a lot of things now, like refusing to take the route where the crash happened, only riding in the car if my daughter takes side streets, and stopping my senior classes and walking club. At the same time, that empty memory blank and feeling constantly disconnected and foggy in a dream are also deeply distressing to me.\n\nDoctor: Can you clarify if the feeling of being in a 'foggy dream' and detached from your life is primarily related to the memory gap of the accident, or if it's a more general feeling that persists even when you're not thinking about the accident?\n\nPatient: It is definitely a more general, persistent feeling that stays with me throughout the day, even when I am not thinking about the accident. I can be doing normal things like looking at my own hands in my house, or trying to follow a recipe or a passage at Bible study, and everything still feels completely unreal. It just feels like I am constantly watching my life from a distance during my daily routine.\n\nDoctor: Do you feel like the foggy dream state and detachment from your life are directly triggered by reminders of the accident, or are they more of a constant, background feeling that you've had since the accident?\n\nPatient: It is definitely more of a constant, background feeling that has been there almost all the time, rather than just being triggered by reminders of the crash. On one hand, my surroundings like my house feel like a foggy dream that isn't quite real. But on the other hand, my own hands don't feel like they belong to me, and I feel like I'm just watching my life from a distance.\n\nDoctor: Can you describe if there are any specific aspects of your identity or sense of self that feel altered or unreal to you, beyond just the general feeling of detachment and being in a 'foggy dream'?\n\nPatient: Yes, it is my own body that feels so disconnected. I will look down at my own hands and feel like they aren't mine, and I often catch myself thinking, \"Is this really happening to me?\" as I watch my life from a distance.\n\nDoctor: Have you ever felt like you're going to snap out of this foggy dream state, or does it feel like it's going to be a permanent part of your life now?\n\nPatient: No, it doesn't feel like I am going to snap out of it, because this foggy dream has been happening constantly ever since the accident a little over two weeks ago without letting up. Since it hasn't improved at all, I am starting to worry that it might never go away. It is very worrying to think this might be how things are from now on.\n\nDoctor: Can you tell me if the feeling of detachment from your body and surroundings is more bothersome to you than the memory gap of the accident, or are they equally distressing in different ways?\n\nPatient: They are both deeply distressing to me, just in very different ways, dear. The memory gap is so frustrating because I keep trying to replay the accident in my mind, but there's just this blank space where it should be. The detachment is so unsettling and surreal, like I'm moving through a foggy dream and watching my life from a distance.\n\nDoctor: Can you tell me if your feeling of being detached from your life and body is something that you feel is happening to you, or if it's something that you're observing from outside, and is this feeling related to the memory gap of the accident or a separate experience?\n\nPatient: It feels like I am observing my life from the outside, moving through a foggy dream where even my own hands don't feel like they belong to me.
